project.title: The Meme Ontology
project.description: Semantic web engineering: an OWL 2 knowledge graph of 5,000 internet memes, linked to Wikidata and queryable with SPARQL.
project.introText: MEMO is an ontology of internet memes, from my master's research Towards an Ontology of Memes (supervisor Fabio Vitali), which I began as a visiting research fellow at the Institute of Network Cultures in Amsterdam, for its Viral Image Cultures project.

project.middleText: Following Lev Manovich's cultural analytics, it treats memes as a large dataset rather than isolated texts. Around 5,000 images and their metadata, scraped from Know Your Meme, are described in an OWL ontology informed by FRBR across three areas: visual content, cultural references and format. CLIP is used to classify them semi-automatically.
project.conclusionText: The ontology is published with LODE documentation, interactive visualisations of formats, platforms, periods and variants, and a SPARQL explorer with example queries, including links to Wikidata for regions and platforms.
project.highlightCaption: Home page: a wall of memes from the Know Your Meme sample, around the project title.
project.context: Master's thesis (supervisor Fabio Vitali), MA Digital Humanities and Digital Knowledge, University of Bologna; begun as a visiting research fellowship at the Institute of Network Cultures (Viral Image Cultures)

summary.brief: A large, messy cultural dataset with no structured model to classify, link or query it.
summary.role: Sole researcher: data collection, ontology, classification and visualisation.
summary.method: About 5,000 Know Your Meme entries scraped; an OWL ontology informed by FRBR; CLIP for semi-automatic classification.
summary.outcome: A published ontology with documentation, visualisations and a SPARQL explorer linked to Wikidata.

facts: memes scraped from Know Your Meme
project.shows: Data modelling and knowledge-graph construction at scale: scraping, ontology design, semi-automatic classification and a queryable SPARQL endpoint.
